The disease is still spreading within the DRC, where more than 4,700 have died. This latest outbreak was confirmed in May. It is the 17th outbreak in the country and the second largest, with more than 9,800 cases so far. Nigeria has confirmed its first case. Reports initially said that the patient had contracted the disease in Uganda, but this has been denied by Ugandan authorities, who declared the country free of the virus in July (News 31 July). Uganda has introduced strict new border controls in the past few days. Ugandans who have visited the DRC will have to undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own expense, the country’s Minister of Health announced on Sunday. Kenya also announced its second death from the virus, and said that seven people were being treated in isolation. All those affected were within one cluster, the Kenyan Ministry of Health reported. The latest outbreak of the virus is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, for which there is yet no approved vaccine or treatment, although vaccine trials are under way. Transmission rates in October have averaged 71 new cases each day in the DRC and cases have now been found in an eighth province. The World Health Organization (WHO) said that containing the disease was “becoming increasingly challenging”. Its latest update report said: “These developments highlight the widening international dimension and the growing complexity of the outbreak, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where escalating insecurity, population displacement, and restricted humanitarian access threaten to further undermine surveillance and response operations.” Misinformation about the virus and its spread led to a deadly attack on a nurse at the weekend in the DRC. On social media, the director-general the WHO, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned: “Healthcare workers must always be protected,” he said. Advertisement The nurse was killed and another healthcare worker was severely injured while responding to an alert, it is reported. Reports suggest that they were attacked by residents who accused them of contaminating a local water source. It is the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders. The UN’s World Food Programme is delivering food to affected regions to ensure that families “do not have to choose between following health guidance and finding food”, including supplying food to those isolating. It estimates that nearly 3.5 million people face crisis-level hunger or worse in areas affected by the Ebola virus. Tearfund’s country director for the DRC, Poppy Anguandia, said: “We are approaching more grim milestones with a likely total of 10,000 Ebola-virus-disease confirmed cases and 5,000 deaths on the horizon in the coming weeks. We’re doing everything we can to slow rates of infection and help to contain the spread of disease.” Tearfund is working with church leaders to raise awareness of measures to combat the disease, install hand-washing stations, and counter widespread misinformation. The Christian charity Samaritan’s Purse has set up two treatment centres in the DRC. The Ebola Treatment Centre in Bunia has admitted more than 760 patients and in Nyankunde, 600 patients. So far, 1,080 patients have been discharged from the two centres. Conflict is making it harder to combat the rapid spread of the disease. Tens of thousands of people have been displaced from their homes by violence. Cuts to aid from the United States and the UK have also affected healthcare systems. Nurse Leontine Kapara Acikani told Tearfund that lack of proper equipment, including personal protective equipment, was the greatest difficulty during the outbreak. “We need to have complete protective equipment when we go into the community. Ebola is contagious, and, if we are not properly protected, we can become infected. The disease is still spreading within the DRC, where more than 4,700 have died. This latest outbreak was confirmed in May. It is the 17th outbreak in the country and the second largest, with more than 9,800 cases so far. Nigeria has confirmed its first case. Reports initially said that the patient had contracted the disease in Uganda, but this has been denied by Ugandan authorities, who declared the country free of the virus in July (News 31 July). Uganda has introduced strict new border controls in the past few days. Ugandans who have visited the DRC will have to undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own expense, the country’s Minister of Health announced on Sunday. Kenya also announced its second death from the virus, and said that seven people were being treated in isolation. All those affected were within one cluster, the Kenyan Ministry of Health reported. The latest outbreak of the virus is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, for which there is yet no approved vaccine or treatment, although vaccine trials are under way. Transmission rates in October have averaged 71 new cases each day in the DRC and cases have now been found in an eighth province. The World Health Organization (WHO) said that containing the disease was “becoming increasingly challenging”. Its latest update report said: “These developments highlight the widening international dimension and the growing complexity of the outbreak, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where escalating insecurity, population displacement, and restricted humanitarian access threaten to further undermine surveillance and response operations.” Misinformation about the virus and its spread led to a deadly attack on a nurse at the weekend in the DRC. On social media, the director-general the WHO, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned: “Healthcare workers must always be protected,” he said. Advertisement The nurse was killed and another healthcare worker was severely injured while responding to an alert, it is reported. Reports suggest that they were attacked by residents who accused them of contaminating a local water source. It is the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders. The UN’s World Food Programme is delivering food to affected regions to ensure that families “do not have to choose between following health guidance and finding food”, including supplying food to those isolating. It estimates that nearly 3.5 million people face crisis-level hunger or worse in areas affected by the Ebola virus. Tearfund’s country director for the DRC, Poppy Anguandia, said: “We are approaching more grim milestones with a likely total of 10,000 Ebola-virus-disease confirmed cases and 5,000 deaths on the horizon in the coming weeks. We’re doing everything we can to slow rates of infection and help to contain the spread of disease.” Tearfund is working with church leaders to raise awareness of measures to combat the disease, install hand-washing stations, and counter widespread misinformation. The Christian charity Samaritan’s Purse has set up two treatment centres in the DRC. The Ebola Treatment Centre in Bunia has admitted more than 760 patients and in Nyankunde, 600 patients. So far, 1,080 patients have been discharged from the two centres. Conflict is making it harder to combat the rapid spread of the disease. Tens of thousands of people have been displaced from their homes by violence. Cuts to aid from the United States and the UK have also affected healthcare systems. Nurse Leontine Kapara Acikani told Tearfund that lack of proper equipment, including personal protective equipment, was the greatest difficulty during the outbreak. “We need to have complete protective equipment when we go into the community. Ebola is contagious, and, if we are not properly protected, we can become infected. Edd Gumban MANILA, Philippines — The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has imposed additional travel requirements for US-bound travelers due to the Ebola outbreak in the Republic of the Congo, according to the Bureau of Quarantine. In an advisory, the BOQ said passengers traveling by air to the US must complete a mandatory attestation confirming that they have not traveled to the Republic of the Congo during the preceding 21 days. The requirement covers passengers who transit through any airport in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, regardless of whether they disembark from the aircraft or leave the airport premises. The BOQ said all airlines operating flights to the US have issued travel advisories and are adapting passenger procedures to comply with the CDC requirement. The quarantine bureau advised travelers to coordinate directly with their airlines regarding applicable attestation and documentation requirements. “Declare your complete travel history, including countries visited and transited within the past 21 days,” the BOQ said. The Department of Health assured the public that the Philippines remains free of the Ebola virus, saying health authorities are on alert amid global monitoring efforts. In May, the World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern linked to the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus in parts of Africa. Edd Gumban MANILA, Philippines — The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has imposed additional travel requirements for US-bound travelers due to the Ebola outbreak in the Republic of the Congo, according to the Bureau of Quarantine. In an advisory, the BOQ said passengers traveling by air to the US must complete a mandatory attestation confirming that they have not traveled to the Republic of the Congo during the preceding 21 days. The requirement covers passengers who transit through any airport in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, regardless of whether they disembark from the aircraft or leave the airport premises. The BOQ said all airlines operating flights to the US have issued travel advisories and are adapting passenger procedures to comply with the CDC requirement. The quarantine bureau advised travelers to coordinate directly with their airlines regarding applicable attestation and documentation requirements. “Declare your complete travel history, including countries visited and transited within the past 21 days,” the BOQ said. The Department of Health assured the public that the Philippines remains free of the Ebola virus, saying health authorities are on alert amid global monitoring efforts. In May, the World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern linked to the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus in parts of Africa. analysis.time: The outbreak was reported to have killed over 5,300 people as of November 2, 2026, with cases in Kenya and Nigeria in October 2026. The event date is October 2026, with the publication date being November 2, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak primarily affected the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with neighboring Uganda and Kenya also reporting cases. Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, had a case involving a Swiss woman. The affected population includes individuals who traveled from the DRC and those in close contact with infected persons.
analysis.event: Ebola virus disease caused a rapidly growing outbreak, resulting in over 5,300 deaths. The outbreak was confirmed by health authorities, with cases reported in multiple countries, including Kenya and Nigeria, involving individuals who had traveled from the DRC.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak resulted in over 5,300 deaths, with Kenya reporting nine infections and Nigeria one case in October 2026. The health system in the DRC and neighboring countries faced significant strain due to the rapid spread of the disease. The risk was described as high due to the potential for further transmission and the challenges in containment.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health authorities in the DRC and neighboring countries were actively investigating and responding to the outbreak. Contact tracing and isolation measures were implemented, but the situation remained under investigation due to the complexity of tracking transmission and the challenges in controlling the spread.

analysis.brief_en: The news report highlights the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, with over 5,300 deaths reported as of November 2, 2026. Kenya reported nine infections in October 2026, marking the first time the country had seen an Ebola case. The outbreak has placed significant strain on the health systems of the DRC and other affected regions. Health authorities are conducting investigations, implementing contact tracing, and isolating infected individuals to contain the spread. The situation remains under active scrutiny due to the challenges in managing such a large-scale outbreak.

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 暴发 主要影响刚果民主共和国 (DRC),邻国乌干达和肯尼亚也报告了病例。非洲人口最多的国家尼日利亚曾发生一起涉及一名瑞士妇女的案件。受影响人群包括来自刚果民主共和国的个人以及与感染者有密切接触的人。
analysis_zh.event: 埃博拉病毒病 导致 暴发 迅速增长,导致 5,300 多人死亡。暴发 得到了卫生当局的证实,包括肯尼亚和尼日利亚在内的多个国家报告了病例,涉及来自刚果民主共和国的人员。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 2026 年 10 月,暴发 导致 5,300 多人死亡,其中肯尼亚报告了 9 例感染病例,尼日利亚报告了 1 例病例。由于该疾病的迅速传播,刚果民主共和国和邻国的卫生系统面临着巨大压力。由于存在进一步 传播 的可能性以及遏制方面的挑战,风险被描述为高。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 刚果民主共和国和邻国的卫生当局正在积极调查和应对 暴发。已实施接触者追踪和隔离措施,但由于追踪 传播 的复杂性以及控制传播的挑战,情况仍在调查中。

(is associated with: «Congo's Ebola death toll surpasses 5,000 as virus continues to spread») Kitsa Musayi/dpa More than 5,000 people have died from Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since the latest outbreak of the virus was detected in mid-May, according to the country's health authorities. A total of 5,026 deaths have been confirmed, while the number of infections has risen to 10,351, the authorities said. Currently, 1,101 people are receiving treatment or undergoing quarantine. Another 2,788 people who previously contracted the disease have recovered. The actual toll could be higher, as experts believe the virus may have been spreading undetected since at least February, several months before the outbreak was officially declared on May 15. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, has been spreading in Congo at an alarming rate. Cases have also been reported in other countries including Kenya, linked to a Kenyan national who contracted the disease in Congo and has since died. Nigeria reported its first Ebola case on October 20, a Swiss woman who fell ill several days after returning from a weeks-long trip to Uganda. Europe has recorded one case so far: a doctor who tested positive in France in June after a humanitarian mission in eastern Congo. The doctor later recovered and was discharged from hospital. Ebola is a life-threatening disease transmitted through direct contact with infected people or their bodily fluids. It can cause severe fever, diarrhoea and bleeding. Advertisement Advertisement The current outbreak has been particularly difficult to contain because there is no vaccine or specific treatment approved for the Bundibugyo strain. Early symptoms can also be mistaken for other illnesses, such as malaria, potentially delaying the isolation and treatment of patients. Clinical trials of two antiviral treatments have been under way since July. Researchers are also testing vaccines, including whether Ervebo, an existing Ebola vaccine, offers protection against the Bundibugyo strain. Ervebo is currently approved and recommended only for protection against the Ebola virus disease caused by the Zaire strain. news.title_original: Congo's Ebola death toll surpasses 5,000 as virus continues to spread

analysis.time: The outbreak was detected in mid-May 2026, and the death toll surpassed 5,000 by October 31, 2026. The publication date is October 30, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The Democratic Republic of the Congo, with cases also reported in Kenya and Nigeria. The affected population includes over 10,351 infections and 5,026 confirmed deaths.
analysis.event: Congo's Ebola death toll surpassed 5,000 since the outbreak was detected in mid-May 2026, as reported by the country's health authorities. The event is confirmed.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: More than 5,000 deaths have been confirmed, with 10,351 infections. The actual toll could be higher due to potential undetected spread since February. The outbreak is spreading rapidly and has been linked to cases in Kenya and Nigeria. The Bundibugyo strain is responsible, and there is no approved vaccine or treatment for it. Early symptoms may be mistaken for other illnesses, delaying isolation and treatment.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health authorities are managing the outbreak, with 1,101 people currently in treatment or quarantine. Clinical trials of antiviral treatments have been ongoing since July, and vaccine testing is also underway. The situation remains under investigation, with uncertainty about the full extent of the outbreak.

analysis.brief_en: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has resulted in over 5,000 confirmed deaths since mid-May 2026, according to health authorities. The number of infections has reached 10,351, with 1,101 individuals currently receiving treatment or undergoing quarantine. Additionally, 2,788 people have recovered from the disease. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, has spread to other countries, including Kenya and Nigeria, with cases linked to individuals who contracted the virus in Congo. The actual death toll may be higher, as experts believe the virus may have been spreading undetected since February. The lack of an approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain complicates containment efforts. Early symptoms of the disease can be mistaken for other illnesses, such as malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment. Clinical trials of antiviral treatments have been ongoing since July, and researchers are testing vaccines, including whether the existing Ervebo vaccine offers protection against the Bundibugyo strain. The situation remains under investigation, with uncertainty about the full impact of the outbreak.

The number of infections has reached 10,351, with 1,101 individuals currently receiving treatment or undergoing quarantine. Additionally, 2,788 people have recovered from the disease. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, has spread to other countries, including Kenya and Nigeria, with cases linked to individuals who contracted the virus in Congo. The actual death toll may be higher, as experts believe the virus may have been spreading undetected since February. The lack of an approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain complicates containment efforts. Early symptoms of the disease can be mistaken for other illnesses, such as malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment. Clinical trials of antiviral treatments have been ongoing since July, and researchers are testing vaccines, including whether the existing Ervebo vaccine offers protection against the Bundibugyo strain. The situation remains under investigation, with uncertainty about the full impact of the outbreak.

news.title_zh: 随着病毒继续传播,刚果埃博拉死亡人数超过 5,000 人
news.source_body_en: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has resulted in over 5,000 confirmed deaths since mid-May 2026, according to health authorities. The number of infections has reached 10,351, with 1,101 individuals currently receiving treatment or undergoing quarantine. Additionally, 2,788 people have recovered from the disease. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, has spread to other countries, including Kenya and Nigeria, with cases linked to individuals who contracted the virus in Congo. The actual death toll may be higher, as experts believe the virus may have been spreading undetected since February. The lack of an approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain complicates containment efforts. Early symptoms of the disease can be mistaken for other illnesses, such as malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment. Clinical trials of antiviral treatments have been ongoing since July, and researchers are testing vaccines, including whether the existing Ervebo vaccine offers protection against the Bundibugyo strain. The situation remains under investigation, with uncertainty about the full impact of the outbreak.

Read more Individual supporters Donate Support us Play Freerice ShareTheMeal app Companies and start-ups Apply for the Innovation Challenge Partners Governments Non-governmental organizations Private sector UN agencies and international institutions Clusters and multistakeholder partnerships Academia and think tanks Goodwill ambassadors, advocates and high-level supporters Donate Home Stories In DRC's Ebola epicentre, food aid and community outreach help fight a deadly outbreak In the Congolese mining town of Mongbwalu, WFP food assistance is helping contain the Ebola outbreak and supporting families whose lives and livelihoods have been devastated by the disease. 3 November 2026, Elizabeth Bryant and Charly Kasereka PausePlayRewind 10s % buffered00:00 07:18 UnmuteMute Settings CaptionsDisabledQualityundefinedSpeedNormal CaptionsGo back to previous menu QualityGo back to previous menu SpeedGo back to previous menu 0.5×0.75×Normal1.25×1.5×1.75×2×4× Francine contracted Ebola twice and lost a child to the virus. Today, she is receiving WFP assistance – spreading the word about staying safe. Photo: WFP/Charly Kasereka From the eastern town of Mongbwalu, farmer and Ebola survivor Francine knows first-hand the destructive force of a disease that killed one of her children and is devastating communities across eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The once-bustling mining town where she lives is largely shuttered. In the hardest-hit places, fresh graves are being dug. Farming is no longer possible. Neighbours and even relatives shrink from contact with Francine’s family. Merchants refuse to touch their money for fear of becoming sick. “Even I am afraid of going to the neighbours,” says Francine. “I spend my days at home and only go out to fetch water.” Since being confirmed in Mongbwalu last May, DRC’s latest Ebola outbreak has morphed into the world’s second largest on record. Caused by the rare Bundibugyo Ebola virus strain, the disease has sickened more than 10,000 people, killed roughly half of them, and spread to eight Congolese provinces and 66 health zones. Even as health officials and humanitarian workers race to contain the outbreak, ongoing conflict in eastern DRC, limited aid, restricted access, and mistrust and misinformation about the disease are hampering the response and deepening one of the world's biggest hunger crises. “Addressing hunger is a key part of the solution,” says David Stevenson, WFP Country Director in DRC. “Food assistance is an incentive for families to seek care promptly and comply with measures that protect their communities.” WFP has delivered hundreds of metric tons of food assistance to Ebola hotspots and supported the broader humanitarian response in multiple ways. Photo: WFP/Michael Castofas How food assistance helps tackle Ebola So far, WFP has delivered hundreds of metric tons of food assistance to people most impacted by Ebola, including hundreds of thousands of hot meals to patients, healthcare workers and others on the frontlines of the health emergency. The WFP-operated humanitarian air service, UNHAS, is flying critical supplies and aid workers to Ebola-affected locations. WFP is also building Ebola treatment centres, and providing storage and transport for essential supplies, including personal protective gear and vaccines, to where they’re most needed. WFP’s assistance plays a powerful role in other ways. In a country where more than 26 million people face severe hunger – including 3 million in Ebola-affected areas – our food support provides a cushion for survivors and patients, encourages less movement of people in search of food, and provides an incentive to seek and follow treatment. “If you can’t feed your family, it’s very difficult to follow health measures that are vital to interrupting Ebola’s transmission,” WFP’s Stevenson says. WFP food support includes take-home rations and hot meals for Ebola patients, medical responders and others most impacted by the virus. Photo: WFP/Michael Castofas Surviving Ebola in DRC A mother of seven, Francine was among the first in Mongbwalu to contract Ebola. Sitting in a dusty compound, she describes falling sick in April, a month before the first cases were officially confirmed. “I didn’t know it was Ebola,” she recalls. “When I left the hospital, I thought I was cured. I didn’t realize it was still in my body.” When she contracted Ebola a second time, three of her children also fell ill. “We were very sick,” she says, describing vomiting and especially diarrhoea. “By God’s grace, we are alive today.” But one of Francine’s children did not survive. Later, she fostered the baby of a couple who died from Ebola. “The family gave him to me for adoption,” she says. “With this baby that I’m taking care of more and more, we’re again a family of seven children.” Life remains difficult. Ebola, along with ongoing violence, has disrupted farming that put food on her family’s table. And like many Ebola survivors, Francine’s family faces stigma. “People on our street began to be very fearful of us,” she says. “They even forbid their children to play with mine, because they are afraid they will fall sick.” “WFP has helped us enormously,” Francine adds of WFP food assistance that includes rice, oil, pulses and salt. Workers erect a WFP-supported Ebola treatment centre in DRC's North Kivu Province. Photo: WFP/Michael Castofas Building trust in Ebola-affected communities Like Francine, Deogratias contracted Ebola early on in April, after visiting patients to offer support. He also became one of the town’s first Ebola patients to recover. Today, the teacher and community church leader credits food assistance for helping local residents to accept health workers and measures aimed at fighting the virus. “This aid has reduced our expenses,” Deogratias says, as he awaits a WFP food distribution. “I think it’s also convinced the people from Mongbwalu.” The turnaround has not been easy. “At the beginning, they thought those people came to kill us,” Deogratias says of the local reaction to health and other aid workers. “Now, they understand these workers come to help us.” Francine agrees local attitudes are changing. She and her family are careful to wash their hands. And she is warning fellow Mongbwalu residents about the dangers of contracting the virus. “My message is Ebola can kill,” she says. Slowly, she believes, local attitudes are changing – and the food assistance is making an impact. “As more sick die, some people are realizing what I say is true,” she says. “And they’re beginning to send suspected family members to the hospital.” WFP's Ebola response in the DRC is made possible thanks to support from Canada, Japan and the United States of America. Learn more about WFP's work supporting people in DRC affected by Ebola and hunger. Now is the time to act WFP relies entirely on voluntary contributions, so every donation counts. Sitting in a dusty compound, she describes falling sick in April, a month before the first cases were officially confirmed. “I didn’t know it was Ebola,” she recalls. “When I left the hospital, I thought I was cured. I didn’t realize it was still in my body.” When she contracted Ebola a second time, three of her children also fell ill. “We were very sick,” she says, describing vomiting and especially diarrhoea. “By God’s grace, we are alive today.” But one of Francine’s children did not survive. Later, she fostered the baby of a couple who died from Ebola. “The family gave him to me for adoption,” she says. “With this baby that I’m taking care of more and more, we’re again a family of seven children.” Life remains difficult. Ebola, along with ongoing violence, has disrupted farming that put food on her family’s table. And like many Ebola survivors, Francine’s family faces stigma. “People on our street began to be very fearful of us,” she says. “They even forbid their children to play with mine, because they are afraid they will fall sick.” “WFP has helped us enormously,” Francine adds of WFP food assistance that includes rice, oil, pulses and salt. Workers erect a WFP-supported Ebola treatment centre in DRC's North Kivu Province. Photo: WFP/Michael Castofas Building trust in Ebola-affected communities Like Francine, Deogratias contracted Ebola early on in April, after visiting patients to offer support. He also became one of the town’s first Ebola patients to recover. Today, the teacher and community church leader credits food assistance for helping local residents to accept health workers and measures aimed at fighting the virus. “This aid has reduced our expenses,” Deogratias says, as he awaits a WFP food distribution. “I think it’s also convinced the people from Mongbwalu.” The turnaround has not been easy. “At the beginning, they thought those people came to kill us,” Deogratias says of the local reaction to health and other aid workers. “Now, they understand these workers come to help us.” Francine agrees local attitudes are changing. She and her family are careful to wash their hands. And she is warning fellow Mongbwalu residents about the dangers of contracting the virus. “My message is Ebola can kill,” she says. Slowly, she believes, local attitudes are changing – and the food assistance is making an impact. “As more sick die, some people are realizing what I say is true,” she says. “And they’re beginning to send suspected family members to the hospital.” WFP's Ebola response in the DRC is made possible thanks to support from Canada, Japan and the United States of America. ByYouri Benadjaoud, Jack Moore, Eric M. Strauss, David Brennan, and Mary Kekatos May 18, 2026, 10:40 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google An American doctor working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola amid the outbreak, according to an international Christian missions organization. Dr. Peter Stafford, a medical missionary with the missions organization Serge, was exposed while treating patients at Nyankunde Hospital, the group said Monday. He sought testing "after presenting symptoms consistent with the virus," Serge said in a statement. Serge, an international Christian missions organization, confirmed today that medical missionary Dr. Peter Stafford, pictured with his wife Rebeka, has tested positive for the Bundibugyo ebolavirus variant in Bunia, Democratic Republic of Congo. Serge Stafford has served at Nyankunde Hospital with Serge since 2023, according to the organization. Two other Serge medical missionaries, including Stafford's wife, were treating patients in the region when the outbreak began and remain asymptomatic, Serge said Monday. "Our medical teams labor in some of the most demanding settings in the world, serving vulnerable communities who have limited access to healthcare," Joel Hylton, Serge's senior director of mission, said in a statement. "We are profoundly grateful for their dedication to the people of the DRC, and we deeply lament the hardship they are enduring under this current threat. Our concern extends equally to our Congolese colleagues and friends in the region who face these same risks." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed Monday that at least one American working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola, but did not identify that person. Dr. Satish K. Pillai, incident manager for the CDC's Ebola response, told reporters that the individual developed symptoms over the weekend and tested positive late Sunday. Pillai added that the patient and six other high-risk contacts are being moved to Germany for care and stressed that the risk to the U.S. general public remains low. Related Ebola outbreak in Africa is 'public health emergency of international concern,' WHO says "Given the previous experience for caring for Ebola patients, coupled with the flight times being significantly shorter, this allows us to get these persons to points of care quickly," Pillai said. Pillai said the CDC has activated its Emergency Operations Center through its country offices in the DRC and in Uganda, and is deploying technical experts that have been requested from Atlanta headquarters. The CDC said earlier Monday that it is preparing to restrict entry for travelers arriving from parts of central Africa where an Ebola outbreak has been declared, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. Non-U.S. passport holders will face entry restrictions if they have been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days. The move is being carried out under Title 42 of the Public Health Services Act, which allows the CDC director to suspend entry of individuals into the U.S. to protect public health. A staff member of the CBCA Virunga Hospital checks a visitor's temperature using a a contactless infrared thermometer, in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo, on May 17, 2026. Jospin Mwisha/AFP via Getty Images The order will be in effect for 30 days and does not apply to U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Popular Reads Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Nov 1 Captain identified after deadly Florida Learjet crash 5 hours ago 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Oct 29 The CDC said it is also coordinating with airlines, international partners and port-of-entry officials to identify and manage travelers with possible Ebola exposure as well as enhancing measures like contact tracing, laboratory testing capacity and hospital readiness nationwide. On Sunday, the CDC said in a statement that a "small number of Americans" are directly affected by an Ebola outbreak occurring in the Democratic Republic of Congo. "The CDC is working with other U.S. agencies to coordinate the safe withdrawal of the Americans," the CDC said. The agency did not confirm the number of people affected, the type of exposure or whether any individuals had experienced symptoms. "We don't discuss or comment on individual dispositions," Pillai said Sunday. "It is a highly dynamic situation, and at this point, what I would say is, we continue to assess, we will continue to keep you posted as we learn more." The State Department said Monday that its officials are working with the U.S. military and the CDC on "potential repatriation of affected Americans, based on assessed exposure and health needs." U.S. embassies in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, South Sudan and Uganda have started "monitoring groups" to track developments and communicate with Americans in the impacted areas, the State Department said. An initial $13 million in foreign aid has also been mobilized for "immediate response efforts," including "supporting surveillance, laboratory capacity, risk communication, safe burials, entry and exit screening, and clinical case management," it said. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told ABC News on Monday that his agency is "working on" the Ebola outbreak. Related Everything you need to know about Ebola On Saturday, the World Health Organization said in a statement that the Ebola outbreak in the DRC and Uganda constituted a "public health emergency of international concern." As of Sunday, there were 10 confirmed Ebola cases and 336 suspected cases in the DRC. There had been 88 suspected deaths in the DRC, as well as two confirmed cases and one confirmed death in Uganda from people who had traveled to the DRC. Ebola virus spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person and does not spread through casual contact or air. Strauss, David Brennan, and Mary Kekatos May 18, 2026, 10:40 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google An American doctor working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola amid the outbreak, according to an international Christian missions organization. Dr. Peter Stafford, a medical missionary with the missions organization Serge, was exposed while treating patients at Nyankunde Hospital, the group said Monday. He sought testing "after presenting symptoms consistent with the virus," Serge said in a statement. Serge, an international Christian missions organization, confirmed today that medical missionary Dr. Peter Stafford, pictured with his wife Rebeka, has tested positive for the Bundibugyo ebolavirus variant in Bunia, Democratic Republic of Congo. Serge Stafford has served at Nyankunde Hospital with Serge since 2023, according to the organization. Two other Serge medical missionaries, including Stafford's wife, were treating patients in the region when the outbreak began and remain asymptomatic, Serge said Monday. "Our medical teams labor in some of the most demanding settings in the world, serving vulnerable communities who have limited access to healthcare," Joel Hylton, Serge's senior director of mission, said in a statement. "We are profoundly grateful for their dedication to the people of the DRC, and we deeply lament the hardship they are enduring under this current threat. Our concern extends equally to our Congolese colleagues and friends in the region who face these same risks." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed Monday that at least one American working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola, but did not identify that person. Dr. Satish K. Pillai, incident manager for the CDC's Ebola response, told reporters that the individual developed symptoms over the weekend and tested positive late Sunday. Pillai added that the patient and six other high-risk contacts are being moved to Germany for care and stressed that the risk to the U.S. general public remains low. Pillai said the CDC has activated its Emergency Operations Center through its country offices in the DRC and in Uganda, and is deploying technical experts that have been requested from Atlanta headquarters. The CDC said earlier Monday that it is preparing to restrict entry for travelers arriving from parts of central Africa where an Ebola outbreak has been declared, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. Non-U.S. passport holders will face entry restrictions if they have been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days. The move is being carried out under Title 42 of the Public Health Services Act, which allows the CDC director to suspend entry of individuals into the U.S. to protect public health. A staff member of the CBCA Virunga Hospital checks a visitor's temperature using a a contactless infrared thermometer, in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo, on May 17, 2026. "The CDC is working with other U.S. agencies to coordinate the safe withdrawal of the Americans," the CDC said. The agency did not confirm the number of people affected, the type of exposure or whether any individuals had experienced symptoms. "We don't discuss or comment on individual dispositions," Pillai said Sunday. "It is a highly dynamic situation, and at this point, what I would say is, we continue to assess, we will continue to keep you posted as we learn more." The State Department said Monday that its officials are working with the U.S. military and the CDC on "potential repatriation of affected Americans, based on assessed exposure and health needs." U.S. embassies in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, South Sudan and Uganda have started "monitoring groups" to track developments and communicate with Americans in the impacted areas, the State Department said. An initial $13 million in foreign aid has also been mobilized for "immediate response efforts," including "supporting surveillance, laboratory capacity, risk communication, safe burials, entry and exit screening, and clinical case management," it said. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told ABC News on Monday that his agency is "working on" the Ebola outbreak. Xinhua News Agency / via Getty Share Add NBC News to Google Oct. 31, 2026, 8:16 AM EDT / Source: The Associated Press By The Associated Press Deaths in Congo’s Ebola outbreak have topped 5,000 as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease and cases are recorded in other African countries, the latest government data on Saturday shows. Data from the Congolese Ministry of Health showed that the disease has killed 5,026 people out of 10,351 infected, at a nearly 50% lethality rate. The surge is sparking concerns among experts regarding the authorities’ ability to contain the deadly virus. The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May, catching authorities by surprise. They have since struggled to manage it. It is already the second deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, second only to a two-year-long West Africa outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people across multiple countries. “It is a very tragic milestone because it is just not a number,” said Dr. Patrick Otim, a program area manager with the World Health Organization. “It is families and communities that have been devastated by this outbreak. The number also shows the severity of this outbreak.” 2,788 people have recovered from the virus so far. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or treatment, but health workers treat patients based on symptoms. Since May, the disease has spread to 67 out of the country’s 178 health zones in eight of 26 provinces. Fifty of the affected 67 health zones have active cases. The virus has been concentrated in the eastern region of Congo, especially in Ituri and North Kivu, which have emerged as the epicenters with 9,782 total confirmed cases and 4,792 total deaths. Authorities are still struggling with tracing contacts and testing, key components in the race to curb the outbreak. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 80% of new cases are coming from outside the chain of monitored contacts, meaning an overwhelming share of infections are coming from unknown chains of transmission to health authorities. Also, one-third of recorded deaths are victims who have died outside of treatment centers, before being tested for Ebola, WHO’s Otim said. These issues, health officials say, contribute to community transmission outside of the immediate purview of health workers who can effectively manage infection in accordance with medical protocols. “These are people we never had opportunity to try to save them and it is one of the biggest concerns for us in this outbreak. How do we try to reach people early to get them to come to health facilities to get a fighting chance to survive?” Otim said. The explosive number of infections in Congo comes on the heels of a long list of issues that have hamstrung efforts to contain the outbreak. The eastern region of Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, plays host to a conflict between the government and an array of armed groups, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group, and there is also an Islamist insurgency in the border areas with Uganda, where the Allied Democratic Forces carry out attacks, limiting the reach of healthcare workers. Also, there is widespread disbelief among the population, which has led to a series of attacks on health workers and health facilities. A nurse was killed while responding to an Ebola alert last week, and a politician from the ruling party was killed in September after advocating for health measures on the radio. Health workers have gone on multiple strikes, shutting down facilities where they treat infected people, citing long delays in payments by the government. On Friday, workers at an Ebola treatment center in Tchomia, in Ituri, downed tools, demanding four months of unpaid wages. At the center, there are currently five confirmed Ebola patients and 10 suspected cases under care. “We are tired of requesting our salaries. If they want to pay us, they will. ... Today, being able to feed our families has become a real problem,” Moise Mugenyi, one of the striking workers, told the AP. Dr. Justin Mukonkole, acting head of response operations in Ituri, said the workers should be patient while the government responds to their demands. Similar situations have played out in other health zones like Beni in North Kivu, where services in some treatment centers have ground to a halt. Alain Siwako, an elected public official in Beni, said cases are spiralling in Beni because of a lack of fuel and financial resources from the central government. “Across Ituri and North Kivu, this outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it, including the communities themselves,” Rose Tchwenko, Country Director for the DRC, Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said. In October, both Kenya and Nigeria confirmed cases of Ebola. Kenya has confirmed eight cases and 2 deaths, while Nigeria’s sole confirmed case had been evacuated to Switzerland. The confirmation of cases in both countries, and earlier in Uganda, made the latest outbreak the first recorded in three African regions and the continent’s most geographically widespread outbreak. The outbreak, declared in mid-May, has infected 10,351 people, resulting in a nearly 50% lethality rate. It is the second deadliest in history, following the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. The virus has spread to 67 health zones in eight provinces, with Ituri and North Kivu as epicenters. Despite efforts, authorities face challenges in containment, including limited resources, community resistance, and attacks on health workers. news.content_zh: 刚果最新的埃博拉病毒 暴发 由本迪布焦病毒引起,截至 2026 年 10 月 31 日,已造成 5,000 多人死亡,已达到悲剧性的里程碑。5 月中旬宣布的 暴发 已感染 10,351 人,致死率接近 50%。这是继2014-2016年西非暴发之后历史上第二严重的死亡事件。该病毒已传播到八个省的 67 个卫生区,其中伊图里和北基伍省为震中。尽管做出了努力,当局在遏制方面仍面临挑战,包括资源有限、社区抵制和对卫生工作者的袭击。接触者追踪和测试仍然很困难,80% 的新病例源自不受监控的 传播 连锁店。三分之一的死亡发生在 治疗 中心之外,这加剧了传播。卫生工作者也因拖欠工资而举行罢工,使应对工作进一步复杂化。

Yes Not now Full Episodes Podcasts Newsletters Live By — Ope Adetayo, Associated Press Ope Adetayo, Associated Press By — Constant Same Bagalwa, Associated Press Constant Same Bagalwa, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/congos-ebola-deaths-top-5000-as-fear-of-continent-wide-spread-mounts Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts World Oct 31, 2026 11:25 AM EST BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Deaths in Congo's Ebola outbreak have topped 5,000 as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease and cases are recorded in other African countries, the latest government data on Saturday shows. Data from the Congolese Ministry of Health showed that the disease has killed 5,026 people out of 10,351 infected, at a nearly 50% lethality rate. The surge is sparking concerns among experts regarding the authorities' ability to contain the deadly virus. The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May, catching authorities by surprise. They have since struggled to manage it. READ MORE: 1st confirmed Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland It is already the second deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, second only to a two-year-long West Africa outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people across multiple countries. "It is a very tragic milestone because it is just not a number," said Dr. Patrick Otim, a programme area manager with the World Health Organization. "It is families and communities that have been devastated by this outbreak. The number also shows the severity of this outbreak." 2,788 people have recovered from the virus so far. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or treatment, but health workers treat patients based on symptoms. One-third of people who have died did not get to receive any care Since May, the disease has spread to 67 out of the country's 178 health zones in eight of 26 provinces. Fifty of the affected 67 health zones have active cases. The virus has been concentrated in the eastern region of Congo, especially in Ituri and North Kivu, which have emerged as the epicenters with 9,782 total confirmed cases and 4,792 total deaths. Authorities are still struggling with tracing contacts and testing, key components in the race to curb the outbreak. READ MORE: Nigeria confirms Ebola case in its capital as woman who arrived from Uganda tests positive According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 80% of new cases are coming from outside the chain of monitored contacts, meaning an overwhelming share of infections are coming from unknown chains of transmission to health authorities. Also, one-third of recorded deaths are victims who have died outside of treatment centers, before being tested for Ebola, WHO's Otim said. These issues, health officials say, contribute to community transmission outside of the immediate purview of health workers who can effectively manage infection in accordance with medical protocols. "These are people we never had opportunity to try to save them and it is one of the biggest concerns for us in this outbreak. How do we try to reach people early to get them to come to health facilities to get a fighting chance to survive?" Otim said. 'The outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it' The explosive number of infections in Congo comes on the heels of a long list of issues that have hamstrung efforts to contain the outbreak. The eastern region of Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, plays host to a conflict between the government and an array of armed groups, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group, and there is also an Islamist insurgency in the border areas with Uganda, where the Allied Democratic Forces carry out attacks, limiting the reach of healthcare workers. Also, there is widespread disbelief among the population, which has led to a series of attacks on health workers and health facilities. A nurse was killed while responding to an Ebola alert last week, and a politician from the ruling party was killed in September after advocating for health measures on the radio. Health workers have gone on multiple strikes, shutting down facilities where they treat infected people, citing long delays in payments by the government. On Friday, workers at an Ebola treatment center in Tchomia, in Ituri, downed tools, demanding four months of unpaid wages. At the center, there are currently five confirmed Ebola patients and 10 suspected cases under care. READ MORE: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases surpass 9,000 as containment efforts falter "We are tired of requesting our salaries. If they want to pay us, they will. ... Today, being able to feed our families has become a real problem," Moise Mugenyi, one of the striking workers, told the AP. Dr. Justin Mukonkole, acting head of response operations in Ituri, said the workers should be patient while the government responds to their demands. Similar situations have played out in other health zones like Beni in North Kivu, where services in some treatment centers have ground to a halt. Alain Siwako, an elected public official in Beni, said cases are spiralling in Beni because of a lack of fuel and financial resources from the central government. "Across Ituri and North Kivu, this outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it, including the communities themselves," Rose Tchwenko, Country Director for the DRC, Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said. In October, both Kenya and Nigeria confirmed cases of Ebola. Kenya has confirmed eight cases and 2 deaths, while Nigeria's sole confirmed case had been evacuated to Switzerland. The confirmation of cases in both countries, and earlier in Uganda, made the latest outbreak the first recorded in three African regions and the continent's most geographically widespread outbreak. Ope Adetayo reported from Lagos, Nigeria. The Associated Press receives financial support for global health and development coverage in Africa from the Gates Foundation. analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-10-31. Event date: The outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026. The outbreak has been ongoing since then, with the latest data showing the situation as of Saturday, 2026-10-31.
analysis.location_and_population: Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Region: Eastern DRC, particularly Ituri and North Kivu provinces. Affected population: 10,351 infected individuals, 5,026 deaths, and 2,788 recoveries. The virus has spread to 67 out of 178 health zones in eight provinces.
analysis.event: An Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus has resulted in over 5,000 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026 and has been spreading rapidly, with cases recorded in other African countries. The Congolese Ministry of Health reported these figures as of Saturday, 2026-10-31.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has infected 10,351 people and caused 5,026 deaths, resulting in a nearly 50% lethality rate. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or treatment, and one-third of deaths occurred outside of treatment centers. The virus has spread to 67 health zones, with 50 having active cases. The situation is raising concerns about the potential for continent-wide spread.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Authorities are struggling with contact tracing and testing, which are critical to containing the outbreak. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted that 80% of new cases are from outside the monitored contact chain. Community transmission is occurring due to limited healthcare access and widespread disbelief in the outbreak. The situation remains under investigation, with ongoing efforts to manage the spread.

analysis.brief_en: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has resulted in over 5,000 deaths as of October 31, 2026, according to the latest government data. The outbreak, declared in mid-May 2026, has infected 10,351 people, with a nearly 50% lethality rate. The virus has spread to 67 health zones across eight provinces, with 50 currently reporting active cases. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or treatment, and one-third of deaths occurred outside of treatment centers. Health authorities are struggling with contact tracing and testing, as 80% of new cases are from unmonitored transmission chains. The outbreak has raised fears of continent-wide spread, exacerbated by ongoing conflicts in the eastern region, which limit healthcare access and have led to attacks on health workers and facilities. The situation remains under investigation, with efforts ongoing to manage the spread and improve response capabilities.

The outbreak has raised fears of continent-wide spread, exacerbated by ongoing conflicts in the eastern region, which limit healthcare access and have led to attacks on health workers and facilities. elements_zh.event: 由本迪布焦病毒引起的埃博拉 暴发 已导致刚果民主共和国 5,000 多人死亡。暴发 于 2026 年 5 月中旬宣布,并迅速传播,其他非洲国家也出现了病例。刚果卫生部报告了截至 2026 年 10 月 31 日星期六的这些数字。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 暴发已感染10,351人,造成5,026人死亡,致死率接近50%。本迪布焦病毒没有已知的 疫苗 或 治疗,三分之一的死亡发生在 治疗 中心之外。该病毒已传播到 67 个卫生区,其中 50 个存在活跃病例。这种情况引发了人们对病毒在整个非洲大陆传播的可能性的担忧。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 当局正在努力进行接触者追踪和测试,这对于遏制 暴发 至关重要。非洲疾病控制和预防中心指出,80%的新病例来自受监控的接触链之外。由于医疗保健服务有限和对 暴发 的普遍怀疑,社区 传播 的出现。目前情况仍在调查中,并正在努力控制传播。

news.content: Ebola cases, AI math breakthrough and the dangers of making daylight saving time permanent Ebola outbreak crosses grim milestone, artificial intelligence solves major math problems, and scientists caution against making daylight saving time permanent By Rachel Feltman , Peter Hall , Sushmita Pathak & Alex Sugiura Happy Monday, listeners! And happy November. For Scientific American ’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup. We’ll start with an update on the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Last Tuesday, data from the country’s Ministry of Health confirmed more than 10,000 cases since May. And nearly half of those people have died. This is the fastest known Ebola outbreak in history. For context, the deadliest outbreak on record, which occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, resulted in 28,000 cases and 11,000 deaths. But that outbreak lasted more than two years, and the current outbreak in the DRC was declared less than 200 days ago. And the difference in their trajectories is striking. On day 187 of the current outbreak, the official case count was 10,060. On day 186 of the West Africa outbreak, just 544 cases had been recorded. There are a few factors making this outbreak tough to manage. The first is the actual species of Ebola-causing virus fueling the outbreak. Of the six known species in this genus, four cause the kind of severe hemorrhagic fever you probably think of when you hear the word “Ebola.” The West African epidemic was caused by one of those four viruses, which is somewhat confusingly now called the Ebola virus but used to be called the Zaire virus, and which has the highest fatality rate of the four. Fortunately, an extremely effective vaccine was developed and deployed to help end that epidemic. This latest outbreak is caused by a different species: the Bundibugyo virus. It’s much less common, having only caused two other known outbreaks in the past. Another factor in the outbreak’s breakneck growth is that the DRC is really struggling to track cases and administer care. The Associated Press reports that at least half of all deaths have been in people who were never admitted to treatment centers. And contact tracing isn’t going well, either. An outbreak is considered under control when 95% of all new cases come from contact with previously known and recorded cases. But at present, something like 80% of new cases are emerging from unknown sources. In other words, there are still lots of people out transmitting the disease that haven’t yet been identified by contact tracers. Distrust of the government and, by extension, of health workers is also a huge issue, with many reportedly believing the outbreak is a hoax . Last month a nurse was killed and another health care worker was severely injured as they attempted to respond to reports of Ebola. However there is some good news, which is that clinical trials are ongoing to find a good vaccine candidate. Last Monday the first participant was vaccinated. The clinical trial is called Tumaini, which means “hope” in Swahili. The trial is made up of people who have recently been in close contact with individuals now confirmed to have the Bundibugyo virus. The first vaccine up for testing is the one tailored to prevent the Ebola virus, but several Bundibugyo-specific inoculations are currently in development and will be tested as well. Now let’s get into some news about artificial intelligence. Just a few weeks after dropping hundreds of AI-generated math breakthroughs on a field that’s already in crisis, OpenAI is piling on more. Here to tell us more about this shake-up is artificial intelligence and technology reporter Peter Hall. He’s currently working as an editorial fellow at Scientific American . Thanks so much for coming on to chat, Peter. Peter Hall: Good to meet you and good to talk with you. Feltman: So could you give our listeners a little bit of backstory for how this has been heating up? Hall: Yeah. So over the past few months OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other players, have really been trying to flex the ability of their models by, um, proving or disproving famous math conjectures. And last week OpenAI introduced these three results across math, physics and theoretical computer science that are quite big. And Anthropic also released the same result, almost at the same time on the same day. Feltman: And so, to give our listeners a little bit of context, what kinds of problems are we talking about and what does this process usually look like, you know, when human mathematicians are involved? Hall: So there’s a huge collection of problems that mathematicians have conjectured or guessed over decades of research. For the proofs from last week, these centered around problems related to Millennium Prize Problems, which are these group of seven problems that the Clay Mathematics Institute published in 2000 as a collection of problems that have existed across math and physics and computer science that are so noteworthy and so important and so difficult that they would get a million-dollar prize for a solution to them. Feltman: So is there any controversy about whether what OpenAI and Anthropic are presenting are actually solutions to these problems, that they’re solved? Hall: Right. So that’s the other side of the coin is that, usually, you know, math research is published in journals or on preprint servers or in conferences. It’s discussed among mathematicians. These don’t really follow the same blueprint there. These are just kind of, like, put in GitHub repos as just a collection of AI-generated text and programming that they claim not only shows that the result is true but also has verified it in a programming language called Lean, which is meant specifically for mathematics. So definitely the aspect of, like, how intelligible these results are and what kind of insights people are gaining from them has been a huge point of controversy—and you know, who gets the credit when a model is just outputting a bunch of ideas that we don’t really know exactly what they’re building off of. Feltman: It’s like when that monkey took a selfie, except I had more respect for both the monkey and the photographer than I unfortunately do for a lot of AI companies. Well, what are the potential benefits to the mathematics community of these proofs being out there? You know, are there any upsides? Hall: You know with previous drops, there has been efforts from the communities to go through the proof, really, you know, with a very fine-tooth comb and turn it into something that is expository and something that we can look at the techniques for and really understand some sort of mathematical insight for it. You know, the hope is that solutions like these and the proof steps, even if they’re not written the best right now, can at some point down the line be turned into something that is useful. Like, you know, I can use the ideas from this to solve some other problem that I’ve seen elsewhere in my research. Feltman : Well thank you so much for coming on to talk through this with us. Feltman : Now for some research on an extremely timely subject: daylight saving time. DST just ended for those of us in the United States—not counting several territories, including Puerto Rico, and the exempt states Hawaii and Arizona,minus the Navajo Nation, which does still observe DST. Complicated, right? And it’s not like “springing forward” and “falling back” are much fun to deal with, either. Research suggests that shifting our clocks back and forth by an hour takes a toll on the body and the mind . So it’s not surprising that this practice is pretty unpopular, and you might have celebrated when the House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July. That bill, which has yet to clear the Senate, would make DST permanent and therefore “preserve” an hour of afternoon sunlight as we head deeper into fall. Last week President Donald Trump blasted the Senate for failing to take a vote in time to implement permanent DST this year, claiming in a social media post that literally no one wanted to change their clocks. While that’s characteristically hyperbolic, recent survey data does suggest that almost half of U.S. adults are opposed to all the falling and springing. But according to a new analysis published in Current Biology , making DST permanent could have serious, dangerous consequences for school-age children. Researchers at the University of Washington who study how school start times impact adolescent health decided to quantify exactly how many more trips to school would happen in darkness if we switched to year-round DST. They found that the Sunshine Protection Act would lead to more than two billion dark morning commutes for children. They also confirmed that fatal morning crashes involving kids aged five to 18 are more likely to occur if the sun has yet to rise. So those additional dark commutes really do pose a risk. The researchers aren’t arguing in favor of continuing to swap our clocks back and forth; in fact, they point out that while permanent DST would be the worst-case scenario for dark school commutes, our current system creates twice as many dark mornings as would occur under permanent standard time. Listen: I’m as bummed out by an afternoon sunset as anyone else. But as long as we can get rid of the twice-a-year upheaval, I’m personally good with whatever . And keeping kids safe as they wait for the bus—or, even better, as they walk or bike to school, because we love a pedestrian-friendly commute—seems pretty worthwhile to me. That’s all for this week’s science news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about how soybeans quietly swept the nation and on Friday we’re going to talk about how AI swept everywhere. Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Sushmita Pathak, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news. That’s why I and the journalists here at Scientific American hope you’ll join our community. Our editors and reporters are often experts in their fields, which means they understand the nuances of big discoveries and can untangle the breakthroughs from the hype. With a subscription, you are also supporting rigorous fact-checking to ensure the words we publish are precise and accurate. And you’re supporting original illustrations, graphics and photos that bring you closer to an advanced laboratory, an ice sheet in Antarctica or a space mission in orbit. You’re helping us craft other types of high-quality journalism as well: Our newsletters are carefully written, edited and curated by staffers you have or will come to know and love. Our Science Quickly podcast is based on original reporting, collaboration with editors and scientists and exacting production. Subscriptions keep this engine running so we can continue to deliver thoughtful, rigorous and independent science journalism to you. In an era of viral misinformation, this work is crucial. Global cities are subsiding by up to several inches a year, an exhaustive new survey shows This bull and male donkey formed an unusually deep social—and sexual—bond The unlikely pairing suggests that social relationships between males are more complex than we thought AI is letting anyone reverse engineer anything. We talked to the developer at the center of it An AI tool called REA can take apart software that isn’t meant to be opened in printers, smart TVs, cars, and more. Its pseudonymous creator wants everyone to get a peek The daylight savings sleep hack you’ve never heard of—‘paleo lighting’ The clocks falling back this weekend will give you the opportunity to sleep like a caveman Do cats fart? news.content: BBC News, Pidgin Waka go wetin de inside Home Watch Plenti seshon Home Nigeria Nigerian Elections 2027 Africa World Sport Entertainment Most popular Nigeria Nigerian Elections 2027 Africa World Sport Entertainment Most popular No suspected case of Ebola for Adamawa state as laboratory tests come out negative - NCDC Wia dis foto come from, Metin Pala/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images Published 31 October 2026 New Informate 2 November 2026 Read am in 5 mins Add am as preferred source for Google Di Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) announce say di laboratory tests wey dem carry out on samples from two suspected Ebola cases for Adamawa state come back as negative. Di agency say di results na confirmation say no positive case dey for di state. Dis update dey come afta NCDC bin raise alert earlier say dem discover two suspected cases for Yola, di capital of northeastern Adamawa state. NCDC Director General Dr. Jide Idris explain say health authorities for di state bin receive one report on Friday afta dem identify two pipo wey show symptoms of Ebola. "Dem collect dia for laboratory testing to establish wetin cause di illness. Fortunately, di samples turn out negative for EBV afta two rounds of testing," Dr. Jide tok. Skip content and continue reading 'Woman wey carry Ebola enta Nigeria dey tok now' - Pate27th October 2026 Switzerland confam arrival of Ebola patient and her husband afta Nigeria govment evacuation27th October 2026 How Nigerian states dey prepare against possible outbreak of Ebola as govment release N10bn 24th October 2026 End of content Two 'new suspected' cases of Ebola for Adamawa dey under investigation - NCDC Di Nigeria Center for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) say dem dey work wit di Adamawa State Govment to investigate two suspected Ebola cases wey dem report for Yola. Dem say di patients dey isolated and tested as samples 'turn out negative for Ebola virus afta two rounds of testing.' Dis dey come hours afta Nigeria say dem don identify two new suspected cases of Ebola Virus. NCDC say di index case wey dem previously confam for di FCT remain di 'only confirmed case wey dey reported for Nigeria to date.' "Anyone wey dey experience symptoms such as fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding, particularly following relevant exposure, suppose seek immediate medical attention and inform healthcare workers of any relevant travel or contact history, NCDC say for dia statement. On Saturday, according to di Nigeria Center for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), dem say dis two new suspected cases na for di Northern region of di kontri. Dis come afta Nigeria evacuate di Ebola patient wey test positive for Abuja back to Switzerland, along wit her husband. Last week, for statement on dia official website, Swiss authorities say di woman dey receive treatment for Geneva University Hospital, while her husband dey for anoda separate facility. Di couple wey both of dem na Swiss nationals, dey repatriated from Abuja, Nigeria, on medical evacuation flight on Monday 25 October, 2026. Meanwhile, dis new suspected cases of Ebola for Nigeria no be confirmed cases until dem do laboratory test. Di agency say both patients don dey isolated, while dem don begin contact identification and also dey do lab test to establish weda di two don contract di virus. "Two suspected cases of Ebola disease dey identified for Nigeria North-East region. Both individuals don dey isolated, contact identification and listing dey ongoing, and laboratory testing dey conducted," NCDC tok for dia statement on Saturday 31 October, 2026. According to NCDC, di classified suspected cases no mean say dem be 'confirmed Ebola cases; confirmation dey subject to laboratory results.' "Di public dey advised to maintain good hand hygiene, practise enhanced sanitation and follow guidance from public health authorities," di authorities tok. Dem say dem go provide more details wen more korrect informate dey available. Dis na afta Nigeria govment don release ₦10bn ($6.7m) in emergency funding to support laboratory testing, purchase protective equipment, mobilise health workers and strengthen oda containment measures, afta di kontri confam one case of Ebola virus. Signs and symptoms of Ebola Ebola na rare but deadly disease wey virus dey cause. Ebola viruses normally dey infect animals, typically fruit bats, but outbreaks among humans dey sometimes start wen pipo eat or handle infected animals. E dey take two to 21 days for symptoms to appear. E dey come suddenly and start like flu or malaria, wit fever, headache and tiredness. Di symptoms include: Sudden high fever: Fever Aches and pains for di muscles and joints Serious headache Weakness and fatigue Sore throat Loss of appetite As di disease progress, di pesin go start to dey vomit and develop diarrhoea and e fit lead to organ failure. Some, no be all, patients dey develop internal and external bleeding. Di virus dey spread from one pesin to anoda by contact wit infected bodily fluids like blood or vomit. How to prevent Ebola virus Di Ebola outbreak on record na for 2014 for West Africa wit ova 11,000 pipo wey die. Dat epidemic kill five times more dan all oda known Ebola outbreaks wey don happun. Di current Ebola outbreak for di Democratic Republic of Congo now na di deadliest of di 17 outbreaks di kontri don face and e don continue to spread. Now, how you fit keep yourself safe and prevent di virus: - Wash your hands evri time wit soap and water - Health pipo say make we wash hands wit soap and water and clean surfaces wit chlorinated water. - No dey touch pipo wey don dey infected - To prevent more of di infection, health professionals advise make pipo avoid contact wit pipo wey dey infected, including for dem to stop to shake hands. - Avoid dead bodies. - No dey kill, touch or chop bush meat. E get vaccine for di Zaire strain of Ebola, wey dey common for di past for Democratic Republic of Congo. And currently no approved vaccine dey for di Sudan strain of Ebola. Howeva, early treatment of specific symptoms, fit improve survival of di pesin wey get am. For medical teams, dem must wear full Personal Protective Equipment, PPE, wen dem dey attend to cases to prevent infection. Deadi bodi dem, for any body bag, must dey buried by pipo wey dey wear proper PPE. Why Ebola dey always come back Ebola dey quick spread. Small sweat or spit from pesin or animal wey get di disease fit infect pesin. According to di WHO, new Ebola outbreak go ever dey happun for Dr Congo because di virus dey live for animal reservoir wey dey for many parts of di kontri. Fruit bats na di main carrier of di disease, but pipo fit dey infected if dem come in close contact wit blood, organs or bodily fluids of animals wey get di virus like chimpanzees, gorillas, monkeys, antelope and porcupines. Di disease dey very rampant for dis area and e no go dey possible to destroy all di animals wey fit dey carry Ebola. As long as pipo dey touch and eat dem, possibility dey say Ebola go always return.
